events.text:
🇺🇸⚠️ Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Ambitions Outrun US Factories
The Pentagon is putting roughly $1.1B into “Drone Dominance,” a program to expand US production of cheap attack drones through competitive trials and bulk orders, aiming to buy about 250,000 by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, Russia is estimated to be targeting production of 7.3M small attack drones in 2026, according to Bloomberg’s October 31 report.
“We’re starting from basically zero,” says Travis Metz, acting director of the Defense Innovation Unit. America knows how to build military drones. The trouble is turning out small, disposable attack drones in quantities suited to a war where replacements are needed every day.
Russia offers an uncomfortable comparison. Russia plans to produce 7.3M small attack drones by the end of 2026. That remains an estimate of planned output, and the American figure covers one purchasing program rather than the entire industry.
Still, the arithmetic is hard to dress up. If that Russian estimate holds, average monthly output would top 600,000 drones. In less than two weeks, Russian factories would match the entire purchase target Metz outlined through the end of 2027.
Drone Dominance is meant to fix this through four rounds of competition, with orders rewarding companies that pass testing and deliver on time. Publishing prices and quantities in advance gives manufacturers a reason to expand. A successful demonstration alone will not keep soldiers supplied.
The second round makes that distinction concrete. Entrants must deliver 120 drones to prove they can manufacture them before advancing to operational trials. Requirements include attacks on trenches, buildings and targets up to 20 km away, despite radio jamming and disrupted satellite navigation.
Then comes the parts bill. Chinese components help make small drones cheap, but restrictions on their use push American manufacturers toward costlier alternatives. Bloomberg’s reporting describes suppliers paying a premium for compliant parts. The Pentagon wants low prices, rapid expansion and less dependence on China, all at once.
Russia’s production advantage makes this an industrial race America cannot win with a bigger check alone. Disposable weapons need dependable parts, repeat orders and factories that replace losses without waiting for the next procurement round. Until those pieces work together, “Drone Dominance” remains a more convincing program name than a description of US manufacturing.

events.text:
🇯🇵💵 Japan eyes record $500 billion defense budget as Takaichi pushes military buildup
Japan's government is considering raising defense spending by nearly 1.8 times over the next five years, setting the stage for one of the largest peacetime military expansions in the country's postwar history.
The five-year defense buildup would be set at roughly $500 billion, compared with the $270 billion allocated for the previous period. Japan has since moved to acquire hundreds of Tomahawk cruise missiles from the US and develop its own upgraded [Type 12 surface-to-ship missiles](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75356), now fielded with a range of about 1,000 kilometers. 
The next phase appears to lean even more heavily on unmanned systems. A leaked draft of the defense buildup plan, reported by Kyodo News, outlined plans to acquire roughly 52,000 unmanned systems over the five years from 2027, including about 10,000 long-range ground-attack drones, 1,300 anti-ship types, and 7,500 reconnaissance and warning models.
👉 According to multiple reports, the Trump administration has repeatedly pressed Tokyo to raise spending to 3.5% of GDP. In turn, Russia and China have spoken of Japan's accelerating remilitarization as a threat to [regional stability](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74965). 
The defense buildup is unfolding against a strained fiscal backdrop. The current budget's proposal leaves a gap of roughly $317 billion that would likely require new debt issuance. To help fund the expansion, the government has outlined plans for a special defense income tax and a corporate tax starting in January 2027.

🇨🇳 China's ship-killing missile back in spotlight as warning to US Navy
Footage showing China's DF-26B anti-ship ballistic missile striking an American aircraft carrier mock-up has resurfaced online, drawing renewed attention to Beijing's maritime strike capabilities.
The footage is not new. The CCTV-marked sequence was previously broadcast in December 2024, making its latest circulation a reminder of China's demonstrated capabilities rather than evidence of a fresh missile test.
The DF-26, nicknamed the “Guam Killer” for its ability to reach the US military hub, has a reported range of up to 4,000 kilometers. Its mobile, solid-fuel launch platform complicates enemy efforts to locate and destroy it.
The footage has resurfaced amid heightened US military preparations in the Pacific, including new Army guidance released in October concerning operations along the first island chain.
While the footage shows a strike against a stationary mock-up, it does not establish the missile's ability to hit a moving aircraft carrier at sea.

events.text:
🇮🇷 Iran key to maintaining Mideast balance & keeping Israeli power in check
OSINT accounts on X argue that the collapse of the Iranian state or a regime change in Tehran could trigger a chain reaction, creating an opportunity for Israel, backed by the US and its regional allies, to establish regional dominance in the Middle East.
Mecca Pact vs Hexagon Alliance
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, who struck the defense Mecca Pact this year, could be challenged by what is called the Hexagon Alliance, or the Abraham Accords axis, experts say.
Experts are grouping India, Pakistan’s longstanding rival, Greece, Turkey’s historic geopolitical adversary, as well as Egypt, Azerbaijan and the UAE, within Israel’s sphere of influence.
📍Turkey’s dilemma
If Iran were to fall and come under the influence of Israel and the US, Turkey would find itself geopolitically encircled by Greece and Iran, leaving it with considerably less room for manoeuvre.
In March, former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett described Turkey as potentially becoming “the next Iran.”
Apparently, therefore, while Turkey may favor a weakened Iran, it has[ little interest](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73592) in Iran’s collapse. Moreover, [Erdogan helped prevent ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72500)Iranian Kurdish armed groups from opening a new front inside Iran, undermining a US-Israeli plot, Al-Monitor reported in July.
📍Azerbaijan: growing closer to Israel
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev skipped a summit of Turkic states hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Media reports suggest that Aliyev is deliberately distancing himself from Ankara’s influence. Haaretz, meanwhile, points to growing ties between [Azerbaijan and Israel](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76494).
📍Egypt walks a tightrope
Despite its energy dependence on both Israel and Saudi Arabia, Egypt is still ideologically more closely aligned with [the Mecca Pact](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71397). On October 26, the Egyptian parliament authorized the nation’s president to provide military support to[ Saudi Arabia](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76980).
📍India
Officially, India pursues a policy of strategic autonomy, maintaining ties with all sides. Iran is an important partner, particularly as a key hub in the North-South Transport Corridor, with the two countries jointly developing [the port of Chabahar](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75919).
📍Iran
Iran and its Axis of Resistance may be seriously underestimated. Alongside its Houthi allies, Tehran retains the ability to exert pressure on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. Some analysts even suggest that Iran could extend its reach as far as the Strait of Gibraltar through[ local proxy movements](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73918).
